lesson_intro.heading: Day 2 at Finova · CSA L1
lesson_intro.board_text:
Users, Groups, and Resetting Access
Finova Technologies · finova-dev

Today you will learn:
• IAM user vs group
• Least privilege — never AdministratorAccess as a shortcut
• Create a user and attach via group
• Reset console password and rotate access keys

You are a Cloud Support Associate. Access resets are your daily bread.
lesson_intro.ren_voice: Welcome back. Yesterday was console orientation. Today you start real Cloud Support Associate work. At Finova, L1 gets the access tickets — new joiners, forgotten passwords, keys that need rotating. We do it with least privilege. No AdministratorAccess shortcuts. I will teach on the board, demonstrate in IAM, then you practice.

whiteboard_intro.board_text:
IAM building blocks for L1
• User = a person or service identity with long-term credentials
• Group = a bucket of permissions you attach to people
• Policy = the JSON that says Allow or Deny
• Least privilege = only what the job needs

Support habit: reset access through groups, not one-off Admin policies.
whiteboard_intro.ren_voice: Three objects matter on day one: user, group, policy. Users get credentials. Groups get policies. People join groups. When a ticket says reset access — you fix the group membership or rotate credentials. You do not paste AdministratorAccess and walk away.

segments.title: Open IAM Users
segments.setup_voice: Watch the console. We start from IAM Users — this is where every access ticket begins.

steps.voice: IAM is global — region does not matter here. Open Users.
This list is every long-term human identity in finova-dev.

segments.lesson_voice: When a ticket says someone cannot log in, first confirm the username exists and which groups they belong to. Guessing policies before you know the principal wastes time.

check.voice: In your own words — why do we look at Users before we touch policies?
check.response_if_correct: Right. Identify the principal first. Then membership. Then policy.
check.response_if_incorrect: Think about the ticket: a person cannot access something. What do you verify about that person before you edit JSON?

steps.voice: Create user. We give a username that matches Finova naming — usually email-local-part.
Enable console password when the ticket is for a human who needs the console.
Do not attach AdministratorAccess here. We will put them in a group next.

check.voice: A ticket asks you to create a user and grant Admin so they can work. What do you do instead?
check.response_if_correct: Exactly. Group with a scoped policy. Admin is a last resort and needs a senior approve.
check.response_if_incorrect: Least privilege. What object do we use so many users share the same scoped permissions?

steps.voice: User groups live here. Permissions belong on the group, not scattered on individuals.
For a forgotten password ticket: open the user, Security credentials, manage console password — force reset, send through the approved channel.
For leaked keys: deactivate the access key, create a new one only if still required, never paste secrets into chat.

check.voice: Someone posts an access key in Slack by mistake. What are the first two actions?
check.response_if_correct: Deactivate or delete the key immediately, then rotate if still needed. Chat is not a vault.
check.response_if_incorrect: Think credentials incident — stop the blast first, then replace.

segments.title: Your turn — open Users
segments.instruction_voice: Your turn. Navigate to IAM Users on your own. That is where every L1 access ticket starts.
segments.hint_voice: Use the IAM left nav — Users. Or search IAM then open Users.
segments.completion_voice: Good. Muscle memory for Users will save you on every access ticket.

segments.title: Synthesis
segments.question: A new contractor needs S3 read on finova-dev. Walk me through user, group, and what you refuse to attach.
segments.response_if_correct: Create user, add to a group that already has a scoped S3 read policy — or request that group from a senior. Never AdministratorAccess for read-only work.
segments.response_if_incorrect: Name the three pieces: identity, membership, and the permission shape. What do you refuse?

session_close.ren_voice: Users hold credentials. Groups hold policies. Least privilege always. Password reset and key rotation are L1 bread-and-butter — document who approved, never paste secrets. Next we learn to read the policies themselves.
summary_points: Identify the principal before editing policies
Permissions via groups, not one-off Admin
Reset password / rotate keys through Security credentials

doubt_session.ren_opening: Questions on users, groups, or access resets before we go?
doubt_session.ren_response_template: Answer using only user vs group, least privilege, console password reset, and access key rotation. Defer policy JSON syntax to the next lesson.
doubt_session.ren_closing: Good. Next lesson — reading IAM policies so you can debug denials without guessing.
